Here, we specifically use the fact that each time we find pair partitions, it corresponds to those terms that survive in the moment expansions. Counting the number of such pairings is essentially counting the ways to group nodes in pairs—an instance of combinatorial partitioning logic.

The table above shows how (k-1)!! emerges for even k. For instance, when k=2, there is exactly 1 pair partition; when k=4, there are 3 ways to pair up 4 items, matching 3 = (4-1)!!; and so on. This perfectly parallels which terms in the expansion of (X₁+...+Xₙ)^k survive, since each variable must appear an even number of times for the expectation not to vanish.

converges to the Gaussian distribution in the sense of distribution (i.e., distribution functions converge). This is the essence of the Central Limit Theorem. In short, any reasonable iid mean-zero, variance-one variables, when summed in large numbers and rescaled, will produce a Gaussian shape.

The moment method offers a combinatorial perspective on why the bell curve emerges so universally. Double factorials count pairings, while Gaussian integrals lead to those exact same numerical values for even-powered moments. Whether you’re summing dice outcomes, coin flips, or any other iid process (with suitable finite variance), the final distributions get forced into that iconic bell shape. Terence Tao’s elegant proof shows that this doesn’t rely on complicated transforms or convolution arguments alone: it emerges from the straightforward counting of moments and the combinatorics of pair partitions.
